entries.content:
Data analysis might sound complicated when you first encounter it. You might imagine large databases, advanced mathematics, and complicated machine learning algorithms.

But many useful data analysis tasks start with something much simpler: loading a dataset, asking questions about it, and using Python to find the answers.

In this tutorial, you'll build a simple data analyzer using Python and pandas. You'll work with a fictional student performance dataset and learn how to load data, inspect it, calculate statistics, filter records, group information, and create a basic visualization.

By the end, you'll have a reusable foundation for analyzing many types of CSV datasets.

Prerequisites

Before following this tutorial, you should have a few basic Python skills and tools ready. You don't need advanced programming or data analysis experience, but you should be familiar with:

  • Python variables and basic data types, such as strings and numbers.
  • Importing libraries and calling functions.
  • Working with lists and basic operations on data.

If you're new to Python, consider learning these fundamentals before continuing. Here's an interactive Python course to get you started if you want to go deep.

Also, make sure you have the following installed:

  • Python: Python 3 or a compatible Python installation.
  • pandas: The Python library we'll use to load, filter, group, and analyze data.
  • Matplotlib: The library we'll use to create visualizations.
  • A code editor or IDE: Such as VS Code, PyCharm, or a simple text editor, along with access to a terminal.

You can install pandas and Matplotlib by running the following command in your terminal:

pip install pandas matplotlib

You'll also need a folder where you can save your Python script and the 

students.csv
dataset we'll create in this tutorial.

Once everything is ready, you can start analyzing data with Python!

What We'll Cover:

Setting Up Your Environment

Installing pandas

If you don't already have pandas installed, open your terminal and run:

pip install pandas matplotlib

We'll use pandas for data analysis and Matplotlib for a simple visualization.

You can verify the installation with:

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

print(pd.__version__)

If Python prints a version number, you're ready to go.

Creating the Dataset

Creating a CSV File

We'll start by creating a file called 

students.csv
and adding some data.

The dataset we'll be working with here is fictional and contains 12 student records across grades 9 through 12. Each row represents one student, and each column describes a different attribute:

  • name
    : The student's first name.
  • grade
    : The student's current grade level in school.
  • study_hours
    : The number of hours the student studied.
  • attendance
    : The student's attendance percentage.
  • score
    : The student's test score, recorded on a 0–100 scale.

For example, Ava is in grade 9, studied for 4.5 hours, has 95% attendance, and received a test score of 82. These sample records let us explore questions such as whether study time is associated with test scores and how average scores compare across grade levels.

Because the data is fictional and small, any patterns we observe are only illustrative, and we shouldn't treat them as evidence about students in general.

But our data will give us enough information to perform several useful analyses. Here it is:

name,grade,study_hours,attendance,score
Ava,9,4.5,95,82
Liam,9,6.0,98,91
Sophia,10,3.5,89,76
Noah,10,7.0,99,94
Emma,11,5.5,93,88
Oliver,11,8.0,97,96
Mia,12,4.0,91,79
Ethan,12,6.5,96,90
Isabella,9,7.5,100,97
Lucas,10,2.5,85,68
Amelia,11,6.0,94,92
James,12,5.0,90,84

Loading the Dataset with Pandas

Reading the CSV File

Start your Python program by importing pandas:

import pandas as pd

Then load the CSV file:

data = pd.read_csv("students.csv")

The 

read_csv()
function reads the CSV file and converts it into a pandas DataFrame.

A DataFrame is a table-like data structure with rows and columns. You can think of it as a programmable spreadsheet.

Let's display the dataset:

print(data)

You should see the student records printed in your terminal.

Exploring the Data

Before analyzing a dataset, it's useful to understand what you're working with.

Viewing the First Rows

The 

head()
method displays the first five rows:
print(data.head())

You can also specify how many rows you want:

print(data.head(3))

Checking the Dataset Size

Use 

shape
to find the number of rows and columns:
print(data.shape)

The result will be:

(12, 5)

That means our dataset contains 12 rows and 5 columns.

Examining Column Names

You can view the column names with:

print(data.columns)

This is useful when you need to reference columns later in your program.

Checking Data Types

Use 

info()
to see information about each column:
data.info()

This helps you identify whether columns contain integers, decimal numbers, text, or other types of data.

Calculating Basic Statistics

Pandas makes it easy to calculate statistics without manually writing the mathematical formulas.

Finding the Average Score

We can calculate the average score using:

average_score = data["score"].mean()

print(f"Average score: {average_score:.2f}")

The 

mean()
method calculates the arithmetic average.

The 

:.2f
formatting tells Python to display the result with two decimal places.

Finding the Highest and Lowest Scores

Use 

max()
and 
min()
:
highest_score = data["score"].max()
lowest_score = data["score"].min()

print(f"Highest score: {highest_score}")
print(f"Lowest score: {lowest_score}")

You can also find the median:

median_score = data["score"].median()

print(f"Median score: {median_score}")

The median is the middle value when the scores are ordered.

Generating a Statistical Summary

Pandas also provides a convenient 

describe()
method:
print(data["score"].describe())

This produces statistics such as:

  • Count
  • Mean
  • Standard deviation
  • Minimum
  • 25th percentile
  • Median
  • 75th percentile
  • Maximum

You can generate a summary for all numerical columns:

print(data.describe())

This is often one of the first commands you'll use when exploring an unfamiliar dataset.

Filtering Data

One of the most useful features of pandas is the ability to select rows based on conditions.

Finding Students With High Scores

Suppose we want to find students who scored at least 90:

high_scores = data[data["score"] >= 90]

print(high_scores)

The expression:

data["score"] >= 90

creates a Boolean condition for every row. Pandas then keeps only the rows where that condition is 

True
.

Finding Students Who Study More Than Five Hours

We can perform the same operation using study time:

frequent_studiers = data[data["study_hours"] > 5]

print(frequent_studiers)

You can combine multiple conditions as well.

For example, suppose we want students who study more than five hours and have an attendance rate above 95 percent:

students = data[
    (data["study_hours"] > 5) &
    (data["attendance"] > 95)
]

print(students)

When combining conditions in pandas, use 

&
for AND and 
|
for OR. Each condition should be enclosed in parentheses.

Finding Specific Students

Using 
idxmax()

Sometimes you don't just want the highest value. You want to know which record contains it.

For example:

top_student_index = data["score"].idxmax()
top_student = data.loc[top_student_index]

print(top_student)


idxmax()
returns the index of the row containing the largest value.

We can do the same for study hours:

most_studious_index = data["study_hours"].idxmax()
most_studious_student = data.loc[most_studious_index]

print(most_studious_student)

This lets you connect a statistic back to the original record.

Grouping Data

Grouping becomes particularly useful when your dataset contains categories.

In our dataset, students belong to different grades.

Average Score by Grade

We can calculate the average score for each grade:

average_by_grade = data.groupby("grade")["score"].mean()

print(average_by_grade)

This tells us how the average score differs between grades.

We can make the output easier to read:

average_by_grade = (
    data.groupby("grade")["score"]
    .mean()
    .round(2)
)

print(average_by_grade)

Multiple Statistics

You can calculate several statistics at once:

grade_summary = data.groupby("grade")["score"].agg(
    ["mean", "min", "max", "count"]
)

print(grade_summary)

This produces a summary for each grade containing the average, minimum, maximum, and number of students.

Analyzing Study Time

We can also investigate the relationship between study hours and scores.

Calculating Correlation

Pandas provides a 

corr()
method:
correlation = data["study_hours"].corr(data["score"])

print(f"Correlation: {correlation:.2f}")

The correlation value generally ranges from -1 to 1.

A value closer to 1 indicates a stronger positive linear relationship, while a value closer to -1 indicates a stronger negative linear relationship. A value near 0 indicates little linear relationship.

However, correlation does not prove that one variable causes another. For example, if study hours and scores are correlated in this dataset, that doesn't prove that studying more directly caused higher scores.

Creating a Visualization

Numbers are useful, but visualizations can make patterns easier to recognize.

Creating a Scatter Plot

We'll create a scatter plot showing study hours and test scores:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.scatter(data["study_hours"], data["score"])

plt.xlabel("Study Hours")
plt.ylabel("Test Score")
plt.title("Study Hours vs. Test Scores")

plt.show()

Each point represents one student.

The x-axis represents study hours, while the y-axis represents test scores.

You may notice whether the points appear to generally move upward as study time increases.

This is what it should look like:

Creating a Bar Chart

We can also visualize the average score for each grade:

average_by_grade = data.groupby("grade")["score"].mean()

average_by_grade.plot(kind="bar")

plt.xlabel("Grade")
plt.ylabel("Average Score")
plt.title("Average Score by Grade")

plt.show()

A bar chart makes it easier to compare the averages between groups.

This is what the bar chart should look like:

Building the Complete Analyzer

Now let's combine the main ideas into one program.

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Load the dataset
data = pd.read_csv("students.csv")

# Basic information
print("Dataset shape:")
print(data.shape)

print("\nFirst five rows:")
print(data.head())

# Score statistics
average_score = data["score"].mean()
median_score = data["score"].median()
highest_score = data["score"].max()
lowest_score = data["score"].min()

print("\nScore Statistics")
print(f"Average: {average_score:.2f}")
print(f"Median: {median_score:.2f}")
print(f"Highest: {highest_score}")
print(f"Lowest: {lowest_score}")

# Students with scores of 90 or higher
high_scores = data[data["score"] >= 90]

print("\nStudents with scores of 90 or higher:")
print(high_scores[["name", "score"]])

# Average score by grade
average_by_grade = (
    data.groupby("grade")["score"]
    .mean()
    .round(2)
)

print("\nAverage Score by Grade:")
print(average_by_grade)

# Study hours and score correlation
correlation = data["study_hours"].corr(data["score"])

print(f"\nStudy Hours vs. Score Correlation: {correlation:.2f}")

# Scatter plot
plt.scatter(data["study_hours"], data["score"])

plt.xlabel("Study Hours")
plt.ylabel("Test Score")
plt.title("Study Hours vs. Test Scores")

plt.show()

This program now performs a small but complete data analysis workflow.

Making the Analyzer More Reusable

A useful next step is turning repeated operations into functions.

Creating an Analysis Function

Instead of writing everything directly in the main program, we can create a function:

def analyze_scores(data):
    average = data["score"].mean()
    median = data["score"].median()
    highest = data["score"].max()
    lowest = data["score"].min()

    print(f"Average score: {average:.2f}")
    print(f"Median score: {median:.2f}")
    print(f"Highest score: {highest}")
    print(f"Lowest score: {lowest}")

Then call it with:

analyze_scores(data)

This makes the code easier to reuse with another DataFrame.

Creating a Function for Top Students

We can also create a function that returns the highest-scoring students:

def get_top_students(data, minimum_score=90):
    return data[data["score"] >= minimum_score][
        ["name", "grade", "score"]
    ]

Now we can change the threshold whenever we want:

print(get_top_students(data, 95))

Functions like these become especially valuable when your analyzer grows.

Handling Missing Data

Real-world datasets are rarely as clean as our example. You may encounter missing values sometimes.

You can check for missing values with:

print(data.isnull().sum())

This tells you how many missing values exist in each column.

For example, you could remove rows containing missing values with:

clean_data = data.dropna()

Or, depending on the dataset and what the missing value means, you might replace missing values:

data["score"] = data["score"].fillna(data["score"].mean())

You should not automatically replace every missing value with an average. The appropriate approach depends on what the missing data represents and what you're trying to analyze.

Exporting Results

After analyzing a dataset, you may want to save your results.

For example:

average_by_grade.to_csv("average_scores_by_grade.csv")

You can also save filtered records:

high_scores.to_csv("high_scoring_students.csv", index=False)

The 

index=False
argument prevents pandas from adding the DataFrame's index as an extra column.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Forgetting to Import Libraries

Make sure the required libraries are imported:

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Otherwise, Python won't know what 

pd
or 
plt
means.

Using the Wrong Column Name

Column names must match your dataset.

For example, if the column is called 

study_hours
, this won't work:
data["study time"]

You can always check the actual column names with:

print(data.columns)

Confusing Correlation With Causation

A correlation can identify a relationship between variables, but it doesn't establish that one variable caused another.

This distinction becomes increasingly important as you work with larger and more complicated datasets.

Analyzing Before Understanding the Data

It's tempting to immediately calculate statistics. But first inspect the dataset.

Useful starting commands include:

data.head()
data.shape
data.info()
data.describe()
data.isnull().sum()

Understanding the structure and quality of your data helps prevent incorrect conclusions.

Where to Go From Here

The analyzer you've built is intentionally simple, but the same workflow can be applied to much larger datasets.

You could extend it to:

  • Analyze sales data
  • Track website traffic
  • Study survey responses
  • Analyze marketing campaigns
  • Examine sports statistics
  • Explore financial datasets
  • Track application or customer data

You could also add more advanced features such as interactive charts, command-line arguments, automated reports, or machine learning models.

For example, instead of hard-coding the CSV filename, you could let the user provide one:

filename = input("Enter the CSV filename: ")

data = pd.read_csv(filename)

print(data.head())

Now the same program can analyze different CSV files.

Final Thoughts

You don't need complicated algorithms to start working with data. With Python, pandas, and a relatively small dataset, you can already perform meaningful analysis.

In this tutorial, you learned how to:

  • Load CSV data with pandas
  • Explore a DataFrame
  • Calculate statistics
  • Filter rows
  • Find specific records
  • Group data
  • Calculate correlations
  • Create visualizations
  • Handle missing values
  • Export analysis results
  • Organize analysis with functions

The most important next step is to practice with different datasets. Once you're comfortable loading, exploring, cleaning, and analyzing data with pandas, you can start building much more sophisticated data-analysis projects.

Happy coding!

entries.content:
A noisy flight can make it difficult to enjoy a podcast or listen to music without turning up your volume super high.

Much of that disturbance comes from the steady rumble of the engines, which continues throughout the journey. Noise-cancelling headphones can reduce this background noise, making your listening experience more comfortable without requiring the surrounding environment to become any quieter.

This is possible because these headphones do more than physically cover your ears. They use microphones to capture surrounding sounds, electronic circuits to process the signals, and speakers to produce additional sound waves that counteract some of the incoming noise. The process happens continuously, allowing the headphones to respond to changes in the sound around you.

But how can one sound reduce another and how do headphones calculate the right signal quickly enough to make it work? The answer lies in the physics of sound waves and the real-time processing that brings this technology to life.

What We'll Cover:

First, Let's Understand What Sound Actually Is

Before exploring how headphones erase background noise, we first need to establish the basic physics of what sound actually is.

Sound isn't a physical object. Rather, it travels as a series of pressure variations moving through the air. When someone speaks or an engine rumbles, it pushes air molecules back and forth, creating invisible waves of high and low pressure.

So a microphone’s primary job is to convert these shifting pressure variations into an electrical signal, just as a headphone speaker converts an electrical signal back into moving air.

Because sound consists of these shifting pressure waves, two distinct sound waves can physically interact with each other when they meet in the air.

This fundamental interaction leads us directly to the principle of destructive interference. When two suitably matched sound waves overlap in perfectly opposite phases, their pressure variations can partially or even substantially cancel each other out.

For instance, if one wave produces a positive pressure variation (a peak) while another produces an equal negative variation (a trough) at the exact same moment, the combined variation can approach zero.

Mathematically, this relationship is quite simple:

ptotal(t)=pnoise(t)+panti-noise(t)

In this equation, p represents the sound pressure at a particular point in space and time. The crucial caveat, though, is that this cancellation is entirely local. So the waves don't disappear everywhere in the room. Instead, the noise cancellation works specifically by changing the sound pressure that reaches your individual ear.

How Do Headphones Create Anti-Noise?

To achieve destructive interference, the headphones must generate a sound wave specifically designed to oppose the incoming noise. We call this "anti-noise."

But it's not as simple as just playing a loud sound backward. The anti-noise signal needs to have an incredibly precise amplitude (loudness) and phase relationship with the original sound, precisely at the location of your eardrum.

Imagine an incoming sound wave that moves up and down like a roller coaster. The anti-noise must be an exact mirror image, moving down when the noise moves up and up when the noise moves down.

Simply having the opposite phase isn't enough, though. If the two waves don't arrive at the exact same time or if they have different amplitudes, you'll still hear residual noise. Because of this, consumer wearables don't generate a universal opposite wave for every sound in the entire room. Instead, they focus entirely on creating a very limited, tiny acoustic "quiet zone" right next to your ear canal.

Inside Noise Cancelling Headphones: The Real-time Process

So, how does a typical pair of ANC Headphones actually execute this in the real world? It all comes down to a continuously repeating signal processing pipeline.

First, external microphones capture the incoming ambient noise. In some advanced designs, internal microphones also measure the residual sound lingering near your ear.

Next, an internal digital controller processes this signal. It rapidly filters the microphone data and calculates the exact cancellation signal needed.

Then, the headphone speaker driver kicks into action, emitting a sound wave designed to oppose the incoming noise (the anti-noise).

Finally, the system continuously monitors and adjusts, constantly responding to your ever changing acoustic environment.

In this process, timing matters more than almost anything else. Sound takes time to travel and the digital system inside the headphones introduces processing and conversion delays. If the anti-noise arrives even a fraction of a millisecond too late, it can't cancel the original wave effectively.

The engineering challenge here is immense: the hardware must predict or respond to incoming noise while keeping its total delay exceptionally low. According to a 2018 study on the active feedforward noise control and signal tracking of headsets, minimizing processing delay is crucial for real-time applications because any lag immediately degrades the cancellation performance, especially for unpredictable sounds.

Feedforward, Feedback, and Hybrid ANC Explained

Not all noise-cancelling consumer wearables handle this processing loop the same way. Headphone designers can arrange their microphones and control systems in three primary configurations, depending on the desired performance and budget.

Feedforward ANC Listens Before the Noise Reaches Your Ear

This setup places the microphone on the outside of your ear cup. The controller uses this early information to prepare a cancellation signal.

The advantage here is getting a head start. The challenge, though, is that the system must perfectly estimate the time required for the sound to travel from the microphone to the ear, factoring in its own internal processing delays.

Feedback ANC Measures What Remains

An internal microphone sits inside the ear cup, capturing the sound right next to your ear, including the residual noise after cancellation. The controller uses this information to continuously correct its output.

Because it measures the result inside the cup, feedback alone has less opportunity to anticipate a sudden incoming sound before it reaches your ear.

Hybrid ANC Combines Both Approaches

Hybrid systems combine the best of both worlds. These systems use both external and internal microphone data to merge prediction with feedback-based correction.

As detailed in a 2019 study on reducing the effects of acoustic feedback in ANC systems, no single architecture is automatically best in every situation. Performance relies heavily on microphone placement, acoustic design, processing delays, and the specific type of noise you're trying to cancel.

The Algorithm Behind the Silence

Let's talk about the software side. An external microphone doesn't just pass a raw inverted signal directly to the speaker. The incoming audio must be carefully transformed using a digital filter to account for the headphone's own acoustic behaviour.

A digital filter uses the current and recent input samples to calculate an output signal. Its job isn't merely to invert every sample, but to output a signal that will successfully reduce noise after that signal has physically travelled through the headphone's speaker components and acoustic path.

To do this, many high-end headphones use adaptive algorithms. Filtered x Least Mean Squares (FxLMS) algorithm is one of the most established in active noise control.

The process is fascinating: the controller produces a cancellation signal, the internal microphone measures the residual noise (the "error"), and the algorithm uses that error data alongside a digital model of the speaker to ear acoustic path to tweak its filter coefficients. It's a continuous loop of measurement and refinement.

Not every pair of headphones uses FxLMS. Some rely on fixed, pre-trained filters, while others adapt actively. But as noted in the 2018 headset signal tracking research mentioned earlier, FxLMS based real-time control remains an incredibly effective standard for dynamic, on the fly adjustment.

Why Noise Cancellation Works Better on Some Sounds Than on Others

If you've worn these headphones, you've likely noticed a quirk: they easily erase an aircraft's engine rumble, but struggle to block out a crying baby or a nearby conversation. Why does this happen?

It all comes down to frequency and predictability. Low frequency sounds, such as steady ventilation noise or a bus engine, have long wavelengths and change relatively slowly over time. This gives the controller ample opportunity to estimate the waveform and generate an accurate cancellation signal.

Conversely, higher-frequency and sudden sounds are incredibly difficult to predict. A slamming door, a loud hand clap, or a sudden shout changes faster than the controller's processing loop can respond. The microphone, processing system, speaker, and acoustic path all have physical constraints that make high-frequency tracking incredibly difficult.

Beyond this, the direction from which the sound originates also plays a crucial role. A 2014 causality study on feedforward active noise control headsets highlighted how different noise arrival directions alter the delays involved, directly affecting how effectively the hardware can align the phases for destructive interference.

Why Passive Noise Isolation Still Matters

Because active cancellation has these inherent limitations, passive noise isolation remains incredibly important. While active cancellation relies on electronics, passive isolation relies entirely on physical barriers, like dense ear cups, tight acoustic seals, and foam ear tips to physically reduce the amount of sound entering the ear.

Unlike ANC, passive isolation doesn't generate an anti noise signal. But interestingly, the two methods are perfect companions. A strong physical seal naturally handles the high-frequency noises (like chatter and sudden claps) that are difficult for an ANC controller to cancel effectively. Think of standard earplugs for studying, for example: they're entirely passive, relying on foam or silicone to block sound. Active headphones rely on their physical design to do exactly that, leaving the heavy, low frequency lifting to the electronic ANC system.

What Happens When the Environment Changes?

The physics and signal processing sound flawless in a laboratory, but the real world is messy. As you go about your day, your acoustic environment is constantly shifting.

If you turn your head while walking, adjust an ear cup, or put on a pair of thick framed glasses, the acoustic path between the speaker and your eardrum changes. Even a slight break in the physical seal around your ear alters the sound reaching the microphone. When this happens, a cancellation signal that worked flawlessly a minute ago might suddenly become far less effective.

Can headphones adapt to this in real time? Yes, but to varying degrees. High end adaptive algorithms constantly adjust their filter coefficients using measurements of residual noise. Other models might seamlessly switch between a set of pre trained filters suited to different conditions.

A 2022 study on adaptive-gain algorithms for fixed filters demonstrated how modern headphones combine pre-trained data with adaptive weighting to handle these sudden environmental shifts smoothly. Real-time processing doesn't necessarily mean every part of the system is rewriting its code on the fly, but rather intelligently blending fixed strategies with live adjustments.

Does Noise Cancellation Remove All Sound?

It's time to correct a common misconception: active noise cancellation doesn't create a vacuum of total silence. Instead, it aggressively reduces unwanted low frequency sound. Human speech, sharp high-frequency noises, and sounds leaking through physical gaps will still easily reach your eardrum.

Some users occasionally report a feeling of "ear pressure" when they turn ANC on. This isn't the headphone blasting dangerous levels of air pressure into your skull. Rather, your brain is confused. It registers the sudden lack of low-frequency ambient noise as the sensation of pressure changes, much like an airplane ascending.

From a health perspective, ANC is quite beneficial, though it isn't a cure all. While it doesn't automatically protect your hearing from loud environments, it reduces background noise, which naturally encourages you to listen to your music at lower volumes. In fact, a 2012 study on noise canceling headphones and hearing hazards found that when people used ANC in background noise, their preferred listening levels were up to 4 dB lower compared to using ordinary earbuds.

While this isn't a guarantee for every listener, it shows how smart engineering can indirectly help protect our ears.

Conclusion

The next time you're sitting on a noisy train or an airplane, take a moment to appreciate the invisible tug of war happening right next to your ears. Your headphones aren't just a physical barrier against the outside world. They're actually actively measuring incoming noise, processing complex algorithms in milliseconds, and deploying targeted anti noise via a tiny speaker to reduce the original sound near your ear.

The sheer engineering required to pull this off is impressive. The internal controller must perfectly account for processing delays, acoustic behaviour, changing noise and the physical limits of its hardware. A quieter listening experience is the beautiful result of several systems working together seamlessly, bridging the gap between physics and computing in a device you can easily carry in your pocket or backpack.

entries.title: Learn Model Context Protocol (MCP) Security

entries.content:
MCP bridges the gap between your AI agents and your external tools, allowing them to send Discord messages, read your emails, and interact with your environment. But this massive leap in capability comes with a serious catch: massive security risks.

Because anyone can build and open-source an MCP server, integrating them blindly can lead to devastating breaches. To help you navigate this new landscape, we just published the MCP Security Fundamentals Course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel.

This comprehensive 2-hour course will get you up to speed on what MCP is, the risks it introduces, and exactly how to use it securely.

In this course, you will learn:

  • The Basics of MCP

    What it is, how it works, and why it is transforming AI applications.
  • Real-World Breaches

    A breakdown of "Patient Zero" MCP exploits and how seemingly harmless community tools can be weaponized.
  • The OWASP MCP Top 10

    A deep dive into the biggest vulnerabilities in the MCP ecosystem and how to mitigate them.
  • Building an MCP Security Program

    The five pillars of enterprise defense, including discovery, governance, identity and access, defense in depth, and detection.
  • Compliance & Governance

    How to navigate frameworks like the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, and ISO 42001.

Watch the full course on the freeCodeCamp.org YouTube channel (2-hour watch).

entries.title: What Is Model Distillation? A Guide for Developers

entries.content:
Over time, knowledge has been passed down in various forms. Before writing was invented in ancient Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq), laws, history, myths, songs, and other information were all transferred from generation to generation orally. This was done either via instructions or storytelling (especially folktales and events that had happened over time).

But another common method of knowledge transfer is from teacher to student, whether formally or informally. We’ve seen this throughout time as well: the Bible recorded that Jesus had twelve disciples whom he taught daily from the start of his mission to his death. Socrates taught Plato. Plato went on to establish an academy in Athens, where he taught Aristotle for twenty years. Aristotle revolutionized science, logic, and politics. And the list goes on.

A 21st-century example of this is deep learning AI lineage. During the 20th-century AI winter, when we thought neural networks were a dead end, this teacher-student lineage kept the dream alive.

Geoffrey Hinton, regarded as the father of AI, ran a lab where he taught Yann LeCun, Ilya Sutskever, and others. Yann LeCun went on to invent the convolutional neural network (CNN), while Ilya Sutskever co-founded OpenAI before leaving for Safe Superintelligence Inc.

While the concept of knowledge transfer between humans is quite familiar, how about knowledge transfer from machine to machine? This is known as "model distillation."

In this article, I'm going to break down what model distillation is. We'll explore the techniques it uses, and I'll walk you through how to implement it from scratch using PyTorch.

By the end, you'll understand how to train smaller, more efficient models and how distillation compares to other compression techniques like quantization and pruning.

What We'll Cover

Prerequisites

To follow along, you should have the following:

  • A GitHub Repository: The complete implementation of the project is available here, and you should clone it to follow along.

  • Basic familiarity with Python and object-oriented programming concepts (for example, working with classes).

  • An overview of deep learning fundamentals. You should understand concepts like epochs, forward propagation, loss function, and so on.

  • PyTorch Basics: While I'll explain each code section for you, basic familiarity with PyTorch tensors and training loops will be helpful.

  • A development environment: You should have Python installed on your machine. I'll be using Visual Studio Code as my editor, but you can use any editor or IDE of your choice.

  • Hardware: For this project, we'll be using a relatively small dataset so a standard CPU will work well.

What is Model Distillation?

Model distillation (or knowledge distillation) is an approach that aims to pass on the learned behavior of a large, highly accurate model to a smaller, computationally efficient model that's better suited for practical deployment.

Distillation is a compression technique where a smaller model (known as the student) learns to mimic the output of a larger, more complex model (the teacher). The goal is for the student model to achieve a level of performance close to the teacher, but with significantly fewer parameters, making it more efficient for deployment. (Source)

Why is Model Distillation Necessary?

At the time of this writing, both closed-source and open-source models are trained on trillions of parameters. These are the internal configuration variables that models learn automatically from training data. This immense number of parameters makes it extremely difficult and expensive to run without proper funding. Models consume large amounts of energy and require expensive hardware.

With distillation, we can transfer the learnings of these frontier models to smaller, more efficient models, making them easier and cheaper to use.

Model Distillation Techniques

The distillation technique used depends on the knowledge that's being transferred. Some methods transfer only the final prediction. Others transfer internal representation, attention maps, reasoning steps, or even the entire behavior of the teacher model.

These are some of the techniques:

Response-Based Distillation

Originally introduced by Geoffrey Hinton in his paper Distilling the knowledge in a neural network, this is the classic teacher-to-student distillation. Before diving deep into how it works, there are a few concepts you need to understand about model training: hard labels and soft labels.

Hard labels deal strictly with fixed categorical targets. When a picture of a dog is fed into a model and it's asked to predict if it's a dog, cat, or horse, it predicts it's a dog, given the result as Dog(1), horse(0), and cat(0). There's no probability as to what percentage or features of the picture look like a cat or a horse.

But we also have soft labels, which deal with probability. When the same picture is fed to a model using soft labels, it can predict that the picture has a 0.85 probability of being a dog, a 0.10 probability of being a cat, and a 0.5 probability of being a horse.

In response-based distillation, instead of training the student model with hard labels, it also learns from the probability of the teacher model's output (soft labels). The student can learn that the picture is a dog, but it also learns that the picture also slightly resembles a cat and barely resembles a horse.

This additional information is called dark knowledge. It enables the smaller model to copy the behavior of a larger, more accurate teacher while maintaining high performance.

Some of the advantages of response-based distillation are that it's easy to implement, it's very stable, and it works well with image classification. But there are some drawbacks, the major one being that it ignores what happens inside the network.

That is, response base distillation only looks at the output layer (the probabilities), so the student has a "black-box" relationship with the teacher model. It learns what the teacher decides, but not how it comes to that conclusion. Using the previous example, it learns the probability of what feature is a dog, cat and horse but not the underlying principle or workings of how that conclusion was made.

Feature-Based Distillation

This technique transfers the internal feature representation of the larger model rather than transferring only the final output.

An easy way to think about this is to imagine that you're a student of a great math tutor. The tutor gives you a math problem and shows you their final result. You might eventually guess the right formula, but you're mostly just learning to memorize output.

But if the tutor requires you to look at their notebook and see their work, you're learning the tutor's exact thought process.

In feature-based distillation, during training, the student model is required to produce hidden layer activations that match those of the tutor using Mean Squared Error (MSE). With mean squared error, the student model isn't just rewarded for correctly guessing the final output. It's also penalised if its internal function system doesn't match that of the teacher model.

This method is heavily used in convolutional neural networks, vision transformers, object detection, and so on.

The drawbacks of this method are that since the student has to extract and store internal feature map of the teacher model at every training iteration, memory and power consumption can quickly escalate. This makes it very expensive to run.

Attention Distillation

In this approach, instead of the student model copying all the neurons, it observes where the larger model pays attention and copies those neurons.

In transformer models, which are models that try to make sense of a sentence instead of paying attention to individual words, attention maps indicate which input tokens or regions the model considers most important when making predictions. The student tries to reproduce those maps or the distribution of the teacher model. This shows the student where to "look" when trying to solve a problem.

The drawback of attention distillation is substantial overhead in both training time and hardware resource. This is because metrics like Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence need to be calculated. These metrics act as a loss function that tells a model exactly how much it's prediction or internal representation differs from the teacher model. Making this calculation across massive attention tensors contribute significantly to resource consumption.

Self-Distillation

A model is also capable of training itself. This involves knowledge transfer from an earlier version to a later version. It can also involve the transfer of knowledge between different layers in the network.

An advantage of this is that the model can become better without necessarily growing in size, reducing the cost of using a larger model to train the student model.

How to Implement Knowledge Distillation in PyTorch.

To showcase how model distillation works in real time, we'll be training a teacher and then a student model using the MNIST dataset and classifier with PyTorch.

The dataset contains about 70,000 greyscale images of handwritten digits. We'll train the teacher, then freeze it while we train a student using hard labels and soft targets from the teacher.

Note that the MNIST dataset is a relatively small dataset, so our distillation gains might not be much. But this project showcases the distillation workflow, and it will give you a good background to run larger datasets.

First in our folder structure is our 

data
folder. This contains our MNIST dataset.

Our 

models.py
file defines the architecture of every neural network used in the project. It contains the teacher network class and student network class. Each class defines layers, forward propagation, and how data flow through the network.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

class TeacherNet(nn.Module):

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

        self.flatten = nn.Flatten()

        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(28 * 28, 1024)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(1024, 512)
        self.fc3 = nn.Linear(512, 256)
        self.fc4 = nn.Linear(256, 128)
        self.fc5 = nn.Linear(128, 10)

    def forward(self, x):

        x = self.flatten(x)

        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc2(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc3(x))
        x = F.relu(self.fc4(x))

        logits = self.fc5(x)

        return logits


class StudentNet(nn.Module):
    """
    Smaller neural network (Student)
    """

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()

        self.flatten = nn.Flatten()

        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(28 * 28, 128)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(128, 10)

    def forward(self, x):

        x = self.flatten(x)

        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))

        logits = self.fc2(x)

        return logits

The 

utils.py
file prepares the dataset and answers the question, "Where does the dataset come from?" Here, we download the MNIST dataset, normalize the images, and create our training and testing loader.
from torchvision import datasets, transforms
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader


def get_dataloaders(batch_size=64):
    """
    Downloads MNIST (if needed) and returns
    training and testing DataLoaders.
    """

    transform = transforms.ToTensor()

    train_dataset = datasets.MNIST(
        root="data",
        train=True,
        download=True,
        transform=transform
    )

    test_dataset = datasets.MNIST(
        root="data",
        train=False,
        download=True,
        transform=transform
    )

    train_loader = DataLoader(
        train_dataset,
        batch_size=batch_size,
        shuffle=True
    )

    test_loader = DataLoader(
        test_dataset,
        batch_size=batch_size,
        shuffle=False
    )

    return train_loader, test_loader

The 

engine.py
file contains the reusable learning algorithm and helps with how training happens. It receives the model.py code and trains it.
import torch
from tqdm import tqdm


def train_one_epoch(
    model,
    dataloader,
    criterion,
    optimizer,
    device,
):
    model.train()

    running_loss = 0

    progress = tqdm(dataloader)

    for images, labels in progress:

        images = images.to(device)
        labels = labels.to(device)

        optimizer.zero_grad()

        outputs = model(images)

        loss = criterion(outputs, labels)

        loss.backward()

        optimizer.step()

        running_loss += loss.item()

        progress.set_description(
            f"Loss {loss.item():.4f}"
        )

    return running_loss / len(dataloader)


def evaluate(model, dataloader, device):

    model.eval()

    correct = 0
    total = 0

    with torch.no_grad():

        for images, labels in dataloader:

            images = images.to(device)
            labels = labels.to(device)

            outputs = model(images)

            _, predicted = torch.max(outputs, dim=1)

            total += labels.size(0)

            correct += (predicted == labels).sum().item()

    accuracy = 100 * correct / total

    return accuracy


def predict(model, images, device):

    model.eval()

    with torch.no_grad():

        images = images.to(device)

        outputs = model(images)

        _, predictions = torch.max(outputs, dim=1)

    return predictions

def train_distillation_epoch(
    teacher,
    student,
    dataloader,
    optimizer,
    device,
    loss_fn,
    temperature=4.0,
    alpha=0.5,
):
    """
    Train the student using a frozen teacher.
    """

    teacher.eval()
    student.train()

    running_loss = 0

    progress = tqdm(dataloader)

    for images, labels in progress:

        images = images.to(device)
        labels = labels.to(device)

        optimizer.zero_grad()

        # Teacher predictions (NO gradients)
        with torch.no_grad():
            teacher_logits = teacher(images)

        # Student predictions
        student_logits = student(images)

        # Combined loss
        loss = loss_fn(
            student_logits=student_logits,
            teacher_logits=teacher_logits,
            labels=labels,
            temperature=temperature,
            alpha=alpha,
        )

        loss.backward()

        optimizer.step()

        running_loss += loss.item()

        progress.set_description(
            f"Distill Loss {loss.item():.4f}"
        )

    return running_loss / len(dataloader)

The 

losses.py
file defines how the model measures its mistake. Since a neural network learns by minimizing loss, for baseline visualize used 
CrossEntropyLoss
, and for knowledge distillation, we introduced 
distillation_loss()
.

Inside this file, we combined hard labels and soft targets using cross entropy and k1 divergence. This is where Geoffrey Hinton's algorithm lives.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

cross_entropy = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()


def distillation_loss(
    student_logits,
    teacher_logits,
    labels,
    temperature=4.0,
    alpha=0.5,
):
    """
    Geoffrey Hinton's Knowledge Distillation Loss

    Parameters
    ----------
    student_logits : output from student model
    teacher_logits : output from teacher model
    labels         : ground-truth labels
    temperature    : controls softness of probability distribution
    alpha          : weight between hard and soft losses
    """

    # Hard Label Loss
    hard_loss = cross_entropy(student_logits, labels)

    # Teacher Soft Targets
    teacher_probs = F.softmax(
        teacher_logits / temperature,
        dim=1
    )

    # Student Soft Predictions
    student_log_probs = F.log_softmax(
        student_logits / temperature,
        dim=1
    )

    # KL Divergence
    soft_loss = F.kl_div(
        student_log_probs,
        teacher_probs,
        reduction="batchmean"
    )

    # Final Distillation Loss
    loss = (
        alpha * hard_loss
        +
        (1 - alpha)
        * (temperature ** 2)
        * soft_loss
    )

    return loss

The 

train_teacher.py
file is to train the teacher network. After running this for the first time, we don't train the teacher again.
import torch
import torch.optim as optim

from models import TeacherNet
from utils import get_dataloaders
from engine import train_one_epoch, evaluate
from losses import cross_entropy

device = torch.device(
    "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
)

train_loader, test_loader = get_dataloaders()

teacher = TeacherNet().to(device)

optimizer = optim.Adam(
    teacher.parameters(),
    lr=0.001,
)

epochs = 10

for epoch in range(epochs):

    loss = train_one_epoch(
        teacher,
        train_loader,
        cross_entropy,
        optimizer,
        device,
    )

    accuracy = evaluate(
        teacher,
        test_loader,
        device,
    )

    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}"
        f" | Loss: {loss:.4f}"
        f" | Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}%"
    )

torch.save(
    teacher.state_dict(),
    "teacher.pth",
)

print("\nTeacher saved successfully.")

The 

train_student.p
y file is where we train the student. It's identical to that of the train_teacher except it's a smaller network and no teacher guidance is implemented here. This gives the baseline accuracy of how the student will perform without the teacher.
import torch
import torch.optim as optim

from models import StudentNet
from utils import get_dataloaders
from engine import train_one_epoch, evaluate
from losses import cross_entropy

device = torch.device(
    "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
)

train_loader, test_loader = get_dataloaders()

student = StudentNet().to(device)

optimizer = optim.Adam(
    student.parameters(),
    lr=0.001,
)

epochs = 10

for epoch in range(epochs):

    loss = train_one_epoch(
        student,
        train_loader,
        cross_entropy,
        optimizer,
        device,
    )

    accuracy = evaluate(
        student,
        test_loader,
        device,
    )

    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}"
        f" | Loss: {loss:.4f}"
        f" | Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}%"
    )

torch.save(
    student.state_dict(),
    "student_baseline.pth",
)

print("\nBaseline student saved.")

The 

train_distilled_student.py
is the heart of this code. In this file, we teach the student using both labels and the teacher's knowledge. Here, we implement response-based knowledge distillation.
import torch
import torch.optim as optim

from models import TeacherNet, StudentNet
from utils import get_dataloaders
from engine import (
    train_distillation_epoch,
    evaluate,
)
from losses import distillation_loss

device = torch.device(
    "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
)

train_loader, test_loader = get_dataloaders()

# Load Teacher
teacher = TeacherNet().to(device)
teacher.load_state_dict(
    torch.load(
        "teacher.pth",
        map_location=device,
    )
)

teacher.eval()

# Student
student = StudentNet().to(device)

optimizer = optim.Adam(
    student.parameters(),
    lr=0.001,
)

epochs = 10

for epoch in range(epochs):

    loss = train_distillation_epoch(
        teacher,
        student,
        train_loader,
        optimizer,
        device,
        distillation_loss,
        temperature=3,
        alpha=0.7,
    )

    accuracy = evaluate(
        student,
        test_loader,
        device,
    )

    print(
        f"Epoch {epoch+1}/{epochs}"
        f" | Loss: {loss:.4f}"
        f" | Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}%"
    )

torch.save(
    student.state_dict(),
    "student_distilled.pth",
)

print("\nDistilled student saved.")

The 

evaluate.py
measures how well a trained model performs. Here, we simply load the model, load test data, predict, and compute the accuracy.
import torch

from models import TeacherNet
from utils import get_dataloaders
from engine import evaluate

device = torch.device(
    "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
)

_, test_loader = get_dataloaders()

teacher = TeacherNet().to(device)

teacher.load_state_dict(
    torch.load(
        "teacher.pth",
        map_location=device,
    )
)

accuracy = evaluate(
    teacher,
    test_loader,
    device,
)

print(
    f"Teacher Accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}%"
)

The 

visualize.py
file is to present our findings visually. We use the Python package matplotlib to visualise the results of our teacher, baseline student, and distilled student.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

models = [
    "Teacher",
    "Baseline\nStudent",
    "Distilled\nStudent"
]

accuracy = [98.20, 97.86, 97.91]

plt.figure(figsize=(7,5))
plt.bar(models, accuracy)

plt.title("Knowledge Distillation Performance Comparison")
plt.ylabel("Accuracy (%)")

for i, v in enumerate(accuracy):
    plt.text(i, v + 0.02, f"{v:.2f}%", ha="center")

plt.ylim(97.5, 98.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("accuracy_comparison.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()

                          │
                          ▼

             ┌────────────┼────────────┐
             │            │            │

             │            │            │

How to Evaluate the Results

Now, let's check and evaluate our results. These are screenshots from running ten epochs for each of the networks: the teacher, student, and distilled student network.

Distilled Student Network: After 10 complete cycle, we attained an accuracy of 98.20%. We had an improvement from 97.74% achieved without the teacher's model knowledge.

Other Approaches for Reducing Model Size

Now that we've seen what model distillation is with real-world code examples. Let's look at other approaches that developers are taking to reduce the size of large language models to save on latency, memory footprints, and compute cost and how they differ from distillation.

We have three other major approaches for this:

Quantization

Quantization achieves efficiency by strictly reducing the bit-width of the underlying data types used to store numerical weight and activations of the neural network. It targets the memory bandwidth bottleneck rather than the model architecture.

In simple terms, quantization can change a 32-bit number to 8-bit numbers, which saves about 75% of the file size.

A real-world example of how quantization differs from distillation is trying to save resources like ink and paper when printing a textbook. Distillation summarizes the textbook, while quantization prints the exact thing but uses a lower-resolution font to save ink and paper.

Pruning

Pruning operates on the principle that large language models often have too many redundant and low-impact parameters on the network. By removing weak connections, models can become smaller and faster.

For the textbook analogy, the pruning process is like going through the textbook and ripping off pages or chapters that you feel aren't needed.

Low-Rank Factorization

This is a mathematical process that uses linear algebra to simplify the matrix multiplication that dominates the deep learning architecture.

With the textbook example, this process involves rewriting complex sentences into simpler, shorter formulas that mean the same thing.

Choosing which method to use depends on the bottleneck you're trying to solve. Quantization generally works well for memory challenges, while pruning and distillation are designed to reduce computation time.

Conclusion

Knowledge transfer is as fundamental to artificial intelligence as it is to human history. Just as Aristotle built upon the teachings of Plato, today's efficient, deployable neural networks rely on the foundational "dark knowledge" extracted from massive, compute-heavy teacher models.

While training trillion-parameter frontier models requires immense hardware and financial resources, knowledge distillation ensures that the practical benefits of these advancements aren't locked behind massive computational bottlenecks.

As we demonstrated with the PyTorch MNIST experiment, even a simple response-based distillation can help a smaller network punch above its weight class by learning from the soft probabilities of a larger teacher.

When combined with other optimization techniques like quantization and pruning, distillation provides a clear pathway for deploying highly capable AI on edge devices, mobile phones, and consumer-grade hardware.

Thank you for reading! Please check out my YouTube channel, where I post videos on AI-related content.

entries.title: How to Diagnose vite: not found After npm ci in a Container Build
entries.summary: I recently worked on a project where a Node.js application used Vite to compile its frontend. It worked in a browser-hosted development environment, but its image build failed after the move to Azure
entries.content:
I recently worked on a project where a Node.js application used Vite to compile its frontend. It worked in a browser-hosted development environment, but its image build failed after the move to Azure Container Registry. The build reported a missing Vite executable after an earlier dependency install had failed.

The container build ended with a simple error:

sh: 1: vite: not found

Vite already appeared in 

devDependencies
. The build stage had run 
npm ci
before calling the build script. The Dockerfile looked ordinary, so the first explanations all pointed at dependency selection or 
NODE_ENV
.

The missing binary came from an earlier failure. 

npm ci
had tried to download hundreds of tarballs from a package host that only existed inside the browser-based development environment. It printed 
Exit handler never called!
, left 
node_modules
empty, and didn't give Docker a clear failure status. The following layer reached 
npm run build
and reported the first missing executable it needed.

The lockfile pointed npm at an unreachable host. This tutorial shows how to check whether the install completed, find the affected tarball URLs, and check the dependency layer before compiling the application. The repair changes the public-package URL prefix and adds build checks. Package versions, integrity values, application code, and Vite configuration stay the same.

Table of Contents

  • Before You Begin

  • How the Build Reached the Failure

  • Step 1: Check Whethernpm ciInstalled Anything

  • Step 2: Find Where the Lockfile Would Download Packages

  • Step 3: Rewrite Only the Known Public-package URL Prefix

  • Step 4: Apply the Guard at Every Independent Install

  • Step 5: Verify the Dependency Tree and the Trust Boundary

  • References

Before You Begin

You need a Node.js project with 

package.json
, a version 2 or 3 
package-lock.json
, its container build log, and Docker. The example uses a supported Node 24 image and a Vite project that writes its build output to 
dist
. Check your own dependency compatibility and output directory.

Check whether the affected packages come from a public or private registry before changing any URLs. The 

.invalid
hostname below stands in for the original internal host. Adapt that prefix only after reviewing the packages it serves.

How the Build Reached the Failure

The application came from a browser-hosted development environment and later moved into an Azure Container Registry build. The development platform acted as a proxy for public npm packages. When it regenerated 

package-lock.json
, it stored its own internal tarball URLs in the 
resolved
fields.

The failure crossed two environments:

  • Inside the development environment, npm could reach the package proxy. The lockfile kept those proxy URLs.

  • The Azure Container Registry image builder received the same lockfile, but it couldn't resolve the proxy hostname.

  • The dependency install printed 

    Exit handler never called!
    and left 
    node_modules
    empty. Its failure status didn't stop the next Docker layer in this incident.

  • The next layer ran 

    npm run build
    , which called Vite. With no installed Vite executable, the build reported 
    vite: not found
    .

The checks below follow that chain backward from the missing executable to the package locations, then repair the URLs and guard each independent install.

Figure 1. The container build reported the last failure in the chain.

Step 1: Check Whether 
npm ci
Installed Anything

The project used 

npm ci
, which was the correct command for a repeatable container build. npm's documentation says that the command removes an existing 
node_modules
directory before it starts the install. It also treats the lockfile as frozen instead of updating it.

Those properties made this failure unusually clear. The build couldn't fall back to packages from an earlier local install. Once the tarball downloads failed, the dependency directory contained nothing useful.

The Dockerfile separated dependency installation from source compilation. Step 3 compares that original sequence with the revised build.

The later 

vite: not found
message didn't show whether npm had installed the package. Start with the dependency directory in the same environment that failed:
test -d node_modules && find node_modules -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 | head
test -x node_modules/.bin/vite

In this build, the first check found no installed packages. The second confirmed that the Vite executable was missing. A missing binary can also result from omitting development dependencies, so inspect the directory before changing 

NODE_ENV
or the package manifest.

After a successful install, the directory listing should show package names. The 

test -x
command prints nothing. Immediately after it, inspect its exit status:
echo $?

For a missing Vite executable, the expected result is:

1

A result of 

0
means the executable exists and is executable.

Checkpoint: An empty dependency directory points to the install step. If other packages exist but Vite is missing, also check whether the install omitted development dependencies. These commands inspect the dependency directory without changing it.

Step 2: Find Where the Lockfile Would Download Packages

A generalized entry looked like this:

{
  "node_modules/example-package": {
    "version": "1.2.3",
    "resolved": "http://packages.internal.invalid/npm/example-package/-/example-package-1.2.3.tgz",
    "integrity": "sha512-"
  }
}

The 

.invalid
hostname above replaces the real internal hostname. The structure matches the historical lockfile.

npm documents 

resolved
as the location from which it obtained a package. For a registry package, that value can be a tarball URL. The configured registry on the build runner therefore didn't solve this incident. The lockfile already told npm where to fetch each tarball.

I counted the affected entries in the historical file. Of 1,038 dependency entries, 528 carried the internal hostname. Each pointed at a host that didn't resolve in the external build environment.

The npm debug output pointed to an earlier failure. The hostname failures appeared before 

Exit handler never called!
. That order mattered. The exit-handler message described how npm ended, while the failed downloads explained why the dependency tree was empty.

I inspected the lockfile as data instead of searching for one package name. This small script groups every HTTP 

resolved
value by hostname:
const fs = require('node:fs')
const lock = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('package-lock.json', 'utf8'))
const hosts = {}

for (const entry of Object.values(lock.packages ?? {})) {
  if (!entry.resolved?.startsWith('http')) continue
  const host = new URL(entry.resolved).host
  hosts[host] = (hosts[host] ?? 0) + 1
}

console.table(hosts)

That inventory showed that the problem affected 528 entries rather than one broken tarball. It also made the repair boundary clear. The package locations recorded in 

resolved
needed to change, while versions and integrity values stayed the same. If the host list includes a private registry, stop here and identify which packages it serves before rewriting anything.

The historical inventory contained this row. The table uses the replacement hostname from the example:

HostResolved URLs
packages.internal.invalid
 528

Your hostnames and counts will depend on your lockfile. This inventory counts HTTP tarball locations, so its total can differ from the number of dependency entries.

Checkpoint: Identify the unreachable host and confirm which of its packages come from the public npm registry. Record the affected count before choosing a replacement prefix. A hostname count alone doesn't establish that rewriting those URLs is safe.

Step 3: Rewrite Only the Known Public-package URL Prefix

Regenerating the lockfile can mix a registry repair with dependency updates. Keeping the package versions and integrity values unchanged makes the repair easier to review.

The affected packages in this application came from the public npm registry. The development platform proxied them and preserved their integrity values. The historical repair replaced its URL prefix before the container install.

For this walkthrough, save the following as 

rewrite-lockfile.cjs
. It changes only 
resolved
fields with the approved prefix. It checks for missing integrity values and unexpected paths on the old host before writing the file.
const fs = require('node:fs')

const oldPrefix = 'http://packages.internal.invalid/npm/'
const newPrefix = 'https://registry.npmjs.org/'
const oldHostname = new URL(oldPrefix).hostname
const filename = 'package-lock.json'
const lock = JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync(filename, 'utf8'))

if (!lock.packages || typeof lock.packages !== 'object') {
  throw new Error('Expected a lockfile with a packages object (version 2 or 3)')
}

let rewritten = 0
for (const entry of Object.values(lock.packages)) {
  if (typeof entry.resolved !== 'string') continue
  if (!entry.resolved.startsWith(oldPrefix)) continue
  if (!entry.integrity) throw new Error('An affected package has no integrity value')
  entry.resolved = newPrefix + entry.resolved.slice(oldPrefix.length)
  rewritten += 1
}

for (const entry of Object.values(lock.packages)) {
  if (typeof entry.resolved !== 'string') continue
  if (!entry.resolved.startsWith('http')) continue
  if (new URL(entry.resolved).hostname === oldHostname) {
    throw new Error('The old hostname remains under an unexpected URL prefix')
  }
}

fs.writeFileSync(filename, JSON.stringify(lock, null, 2) + '\n')
console.log(`Rewrote ${rewritten} resolved URLs`)

When the dependency stage runs the script, its message should match the number of URLs that use the approved prefix. The small test project used to check this tutorial produced:

Rewrote 40 resolved URLs

That test project is separate from the historical application, which had 528 affected entries. Use the inventory for your own file as the expected count. A zero count on an already-repaired file is expected. If an unrepaired file produces zero, check the prefix.

The script doesn't establish that a package is public. Confirm that separately. npm's integrity check then verifies that the downloaded bytes match the lockfile.

Keep local dependencies and configuration files out of the build context with a 

.dockerignore
:
node_modules
dist
.git
.env*
.npmrc

This example installs public packages. A private registry needs its own reachable endpoint and secure build-time authentication.

The first block below shows the affected instructions from the original Dockerfile. The second is the complete tutorial build. It uses Node 24 and the guarded install, so check compatibility with your own application.

Before: Original Install and Build Sequence

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci

COPY . .
RUN npm run build

After: URL Rewrite and Dependency Checks

Use two build stages so source changes don't invalidate the dependency-install stage:

FROM node:24-slim AS dependencies
WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json package-lock.json rewrite-lockfile.cjs ./
RUN node rewrite-lockfile.cjs \
 && npm ci --include=dev \
 && test -x node_modules/.bin/vite

FROM node:24-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app

COPY . .
COPY --from=dependencies /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=dependencies /app/package-lock.json ./package-lock.json
RUN npm run build

The revised Dockerfile makes each part of the install explicit:

  • The URL rewrite replaces the approved public-package prefix before 

    npm ci
    downloads packages. 

  • --include=dev
    makes the choice to install development dependencies explicit.

  • The Vite executable check stops the dependency stage if the install leaves Vite missing.

  • The separate dependency stage installs packages before the application build stage copies them and compiles the source.

The second stage copies the repaired lockfile after the application source. Otherwise, 

COPY . .
would put the original lockfile back into the build image. The 
.dockerignore
also prevents local 
node_modules
from overwriting the dependencies from the first stage.

--include=dev
includes Vite when it's a development dependency, even if the build environment sets 
NODE_ENV=production
. This image is a build environment, so it needs the compiler and build tools. Choose a supported Node version compatible with your project.

The historical lockfile comparison found 528 changed fields, all named 

resolved
. It found zero changed 
version
or 
integrity
fields and no remaining internal hostname. The example script above also leaves unrelated fields unchanged, although JSON formatting can change.

Figure 2. The portability repair changes package locations while preserving dependency identity.

The executable check makes the dependency stage fail if Vite is still missing. Docker stops at that stage instead of reaching the application build.

Checkpoint: Check the rewrite count against your inventory, confirm that the approved old hostname is gone, and compare versions and integrity values before and after the repair. The dependency stage must complete both 

npm ci --include=dev
and the Vite executable check. Step 5 builds the image and verifies the application output.

Step 4: Apply the Guard at Every Independent Install

The continuous integration job and the container image builder ran separate installs. Fixing the workflow runner didn't change the 

npm ci
inside the Dockerfile. The image build received the original repository files and created its own dependency layer in another environment.

The rewrite belongs immediately after the dependency files enter the install environment. Docker's cache guidance recommends installing dependencies before copying frequently changing source files. In the example, the dependency stage has that boundary. A source-only change rebuilds the application stage.

Apply the same guard before each independent install:

  • the continuous integration type-check install

  • the container build install

  • any runtime-stage install in a multi-stage Dockerfile

Figure 3. A workflow repair doesn't automatically repair the install inside a container build.

This placement also prevented a misleading partial fix. A type check could otherwise pass while the image build failed because the two jobs used the same lockfile in separate installs.

Step 5: Verify the Dependency Tree and the Trust Boundary

This repair was safe because the affected entries represented public npm packages behind a transparent development-platform proxy. The integrity strings remained present, and the rewrite didn't change any package version.

The same substitution would be unsafe for private packages, patched packages, or a registry that serves different bytes under the same package version. A portable build should keep those packages on a reachable private registry and configure authentication for that registry.

Before applying this pattern elsewhere, I would inventory every 

resolved
hostname and separate public packages from private ones. I would then compare package versions and integrity values before and after the change. The build should fail if an unapproved hostname remains.

An npm CLI issue records the same 

Exit handler never called!
message after package downloads from an internal registry timed out. That message doesn't identify the package location by itself. In this incident, the tarball URLs and failed hostname established the cause.

Build the image and verify the output:

docker build --progress=plain -t vite-install-check .
docker run --rm vite-install-check sh -c \
  'test -x node_modules/.bin/vite && test -s dist/index.html'

The build must pass 

npm ci
, the Vite executable check, and 
npm run build
. The final command checks the expected Vite output in the resulting image. Adapt the output check if your project uses a different directory. The image in this example compiles the application. Choose a separate serving stage if you need a production web server.

A successful minimal example doesn't validate every dependency in an existing application. Run the same build against the project you intend to ship. When a tool is missing, check the install result and its earlier errors before changing the build tool.

entries.title: Build a Hybrid Search Engine in PostgreSQL: BM25 + Vector Retrieval
